extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on NLP for peer review (NLP/ML researchers, conference organizers, and developers of review-assistance tools)
extracted.subtask_description: Developing, annotating, and using a taxonomy of review 'aspects' (characteristics of a paper that reviewers judge) for tasks such as predicting which aspects a paper will receive and identifying aspects covered in reviews. Focus is on sentence-level aspect identification in peer reviews (NLP domain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect is a characteristic of a paper that a reviewer makes a judgment on when evaluating the paper, which is later used to compare manuscripts to each other and to the quality standards provided by review guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspects are characteristics of the paper (not meta items like Acceptance Decision). They can be general (e.g., Soundness) or specific (e.g., Missing Citations on Controlled Generation). Choose aspects that are neither too general nor too specific to be useful for comparing manuscripts and mapping to publication standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level aspect expression
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect is assumed to be expressed in a review sentence; multiple aspects may appear in a single sentence and the aspects of a review are treated as a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform identification at the sentence level and allow multiple labels per sentence. Segment reviews into sentences (the authors used Punkt/NLTK) before annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude non-aspect terms (decision/meta-comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms related to paper decisions (e.g., Acceptance Decision), overly general tokens (Weakness, Strength, Question, Comment), or terms that are too rare should be excluded from the aspect set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors removed terms deemed too general/specific and omitted terms that appeared fewer than 50 times in annotations. Be cautious: excluding such terms avoids noise but may remove some useful signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect granularity levels (multi-level taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects should be organized at multiple granularities (COARSE: broad categories; FINE: frequent aspects; LLM annotation: raw, finest-grained outputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide and use a multi-level taxonomy: coarse labels for high-level analysis and coverage checks; fine labels for nuanced specificity and tasks like LLM-generated review detection. A hybrid strategy (COARSE then FINE) can be effective for review quality evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: COARSE label set for high-level analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small set of broad aspect categories (the paper groups aspects into 16 broad categories) for tasks that need high-level coverage/focus analysis across tracks or venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COARSE is appropriate for analyzing review focus across tracks and comparing coverage of key dimensions. It tends to yield higher model performance and is more stable across prompts/temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: FINE label set for nuanced analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a more comprehensive, fine-grained set of aspects to capture specific and detailed feedback (useful for review comparison and LLM-generated review detection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE labels reveal patterns that coarse labels miss and consistently outperform older aspect sets (e.g., ACL'18) in tasks needing specificity. However, FINE is harder to predict and requires larger annotation/modeling effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 16 COARSE aspect categories (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy grouping aspects into 16 broad categories used as COARSE labels in the paper: Ablation, Analysis, Comparison, Contribution, Data/Task, DDDDEI, Evaluation, Experiment, IJMV, Methodology, Novelty, Presentation, Related Work, Result, Significance, Theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each COARSE category subsumes many FINE labels (examples: Methodology → Model, Method, Training; Presentation → Clarity, Figure, Grammar). Use these COARSE categories as the top-level labels for annotation, analysis, and modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects related to the algorithm, implementation, method, and methodological soundness of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Model, Method, Training, Approach, Parameter. Methodology appears in a large fraction of review sentences (~35.30% in the dataset). Evaluate methodological correctness, novelty, and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / Presentation (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects concerning clarity of exposition, figures, grammar, structure, typos, and overall presentation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples include Dataset Clarification, Paper Presentation, Term Clarity. Presentation aspects inform usability and readability; reviewers often comment here and these aspects are used for assessing writing quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Innovation (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects addressing the originality, innovation, or technical novelty of the contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Algorithmic Innovations, Technical Novelty, Innovation/Novelty/Originality. Evaluate whether contributions provide new ideas, techniques, or significant departures from prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects concerning the main contributions of the paper and what it adds to the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Community Contribution, Methodology Contribution, Main Contribution, Technical Contribution. Consider whether contributions are substantial, well-motivated, and clearly articulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related Work / Citations (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects about the literature review, missing citations, and connection to previous works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Existing Literature, Missing Citations, Previous Works. Examine whether the paper properly situates itself and performs meaningful comparisons to relevant prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data / Task (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects related to datasets, task definitions, annotation, benchmarks, and dataset validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Dataset Description, Missing Details, Task Definition, Dataset Validity. Pay attention to data collection, processing, and whether tasks are well-defined and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation / Metrics (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects about evaluation methodology, metrics, human evaluation, and whether evaluation supports claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Accuracy Metric, Evaluation Scheme, Human Evaluation. Assess whether evaluation is rigorous, fair, and sufficient to validate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments / Results (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects concerning experiments, experimental procedure, results reporting, and statistical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Experiments, Findings, Improvement, Performance, Result, BLEU Improvement, Statistical Test. Look for adequate baselines, ablation analyses, and clear, reproducible experimental setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ablation / Analysis (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects referring to ablation analyses and deeper analysis of model behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Ablation Analysis, Ablation Study, Ablation Tests, Complexity Analysis, Data Analysis. Verify whether claimed improvements are analyzed and sources of improvement are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory / Theoretical guarantees (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects about theoretical analysis, correctness, and presence/absence of theoretical guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Theoretical Analysis, Theorem, Theoretical Results, Lack of Theoretical Guarantee. Evaluate soundness of theoretical claims and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / Impact (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects that assess the importance, impact, or practical significance of the ideas and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Impact, Importance, Empirical Importance, Practical Significance. Consider whether findings matter to the community and have practical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison / Fairness of comparisons (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects about how fairly the paper compares against baselines/SOTA and whether comparisons are meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINE examples: Comparison Fairness, Comparison to SOTA. Check for correct baseline implementations, hyperparameter tuning fairness, and appropriate datasets for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: DDDDEI (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad COARSE category label present in the taxonomy (original acronym as presented in paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists DDDDEI as one of the COARSE categories; FINE labels under this category may include items related to dataset/diversity/ethics/DEI concerns depending on the authors' taxonomy mapping. Use domain expertise to interpret acronym-specific sublabels in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: IJMV (COARSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: A COARSE category in the taxonomy (original acronym as presented in paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IJMV appears in the taxonomy; the paper reports frequencies and agreement scores for IJMV. Treat it as a domain-specific COARSE category with associated fine-grained labels as defined by the authors' taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: None / No-aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that focus on none of the defined aspects (i.e., do not address any aspect in the taxonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should mark sentences that do not address any aspect as '-' or a None label. Such coverage helps calculate coverage metrics and identify content that falls outside the taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness as a review desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensiveness is a key desideratum for high-quality reviews: reviews should cover the important aspects of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aspect coverage (e.g., COARSE coverage) to measure whether a review addresses required dimensions. Beware of bias: longer reviews or those recommending acceptance may be favored by naive proxies for helpfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity as a review desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity — giving detailed, actionable feedback — is a crucial attribute of review quality; lack of specificity was noted as a problem in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finer-grained aspects (FINE) are useful to measure specificity. Combine COARSE coverage checks with FINE specificity scoring to assess review quality meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation validity & consistency checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple consistency/validity metrics (exact match, BERTScore, Jaccard similarity) and human evaluation (agreement, Fleiss' Kappa) to validate LLM-generated annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with different prompts and temperatures to assess annotation stability. Map raw LLM outputs to COARSE labels to increase robustness. The paper reports moderate-to-strong consistency and ~91% human agreement on COARSE mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-based unsupervised aspect identification + post-processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a state-of-the-art LLM (GPT-4o) in an unsupervised manner to identify aspects from review sentences, then post-process to reduce variation and group related terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because raw LLM outputs vary (e.g., Result vs Results), identify frequent raw outputs as keywords, group synonyms (Clarification and Clarity), remove terms below frequency threshold, and manually check groupings to correct misgroupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling tasks and evaluation metrics (PAP & RAP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define two tasks: paper aspect prediction (PAP: predict aspects to focus on given a paper) and review aspect prediction (RAP: identify aspects covered in a review). Model as multi-label sequence classification and evaluate with precision, recall, F1, and Jaccard similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAP is harder than RAP; test different inputs (title/abstract/keywords/full paper). Use models like BoW+RF, RoBERTa, and GPT-4o, apply focal loss to address label imbalance, and report both COARSE and FINE label set performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect-based LLM-generated review detection (Sintra / Sinter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect LLM-generated reviews by comparing intra-paper aspect similarity (Sintra) vs inter-paper similarity (Sinter) and using |Sintra − Sinter| as the anomaly score; report @1 and @2 accuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Jaccard similarity between predicted aspect sets. Intuition: human reviews for the same paper are more similar to each other than to reviews for different papers, so LLM-generated reviews tend to be more generic (higher inter-similarity). Compare against baselines (SBERT embeddings, ACL'18 aspects) and evaluate across COARSE/FINE sets; FINE often outperforms COARSE for detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation on choosing aspect granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline: choose COARSE labels for high-level coverage analyses, FINE labels for nuanced specificity tasks (e.g., review comparison, LLM-detection), and consider a hybrid (COARSE then FINE) for review quality assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting granularity is a design choice depending on task and user needs. Example: first check COARSE coverage to ensure key aspects are addressed, then use FINE labels to assess specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and sampling rules for aspect set construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct aspect sets by sampling reviews across venues/tracks and time periods to achieve coverage (the authors sampled ICLR 2020–2024, EMNLP23, and NLPeer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment reviews into sentences, run LLM annotations, post-process outputs to frequent keywords, group synonyms, and exclude rare/too-general terms. Manual verification of groupings is recommended to fix incorrect merges (e.g., 'Improvement' grouping different senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid automation bias and annotate carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When using LLM annotations in human evaluation, account for automation bias by asking annotators to provide explanations and consider open-ended annotation designs with caution (high cognitive burden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate automation bias by collecting annotator explanations, using multiple human annotators, measuring inter-annotator agreement, and considering follow-up studies to quantify and reduce bias.
